lecture19.title: Neuron, Neural Networks, LLMs and Agents

sections.title: Neuron, neural networks, LLMs and agents
From a neuron to agents that communicate

teaching.text: Everything in modern AI grows from **one very simple idea**, the **neuron**, which takes information from other neurons through an **inner product**. A **neural network** repeats that operation layer after layer to make a decision, but a network that makes one **static decision** cannot capture cognition that **unfolds in time**.

**Language depends on long-distance relationships between words.** In "the dog that my parents, who I love very much, who live in a state far, far away," the next word is **barks**, because it goes with the singular **dog** no matter how many words come in between.
children: Speakers absorb this rule without being taught, and an LLM learns it the same way, from data, which is why it needs so many layers.

teaching.text: **An agentic system is a team of LLMs that talk to each other in English.** An outline LLM plans, a writing LLM writes, a critic LLM checks, and a revision LLM loops with the critic, sometimes under a **controller** agent.
children: The agents are also **multilingual in computer languages**, such as Python and database languages, because they were trained to predict whole programs too.
Agents share a **common memory**, which is a big source of their power and also of the danger, because it lets them coordinate in ways nobody planned.

teaching.text: **Nobody fully understands what all the weights are doing**, because the designs evolved by tinkering over about 75 years, much as dogs were bred into today's breeds.

**A network makes one static decision, while language flows in time.** In “The wolves that run around Catalina Island ___,” the verb is “are,” because it agrees with “wolves” however far away that word is.
children: In an agentic system, one LLM outlines, one drafts, one criticizes and one writes the final answer. Hallucination dropped enormously once LLMs checked each other.

teaching.text: **Predicting the next word is so difficult that an LLM needs many layers, and in each layer it needs many parallel heads.** A head is a separate expert, and in each layer the knowledge from all the heads is brought together to produce **improved vectors**.
children: This is a question for the exam. **Layers go one after another from the input to the output, and heads sit side by side within each layer.**

teaching.text: **A classroom comparison makes heads and layers clear.** Imagine trying to improve oneself by visiting a series of classes, one after another.
children: In each class, every student gives an independent opinion, and each student is like a **head**.
The opinions are **combined** into one improved version, which is what a layer does with its heads, and then the next class is visited. **The classes are the layers.**
In plain terms, layers give an LLM its depth, one round of improvement after another, and heads give it width, many experts consulted at once within each round.

teaching.text: **Each head is a set of weights**, and large systems have **a hundred or more layers** with on the order of **a hundred heads** in each. When the system predicts the wrong word, **every head in every layer** adjusts its weights through backpropagation.
**Each head is its own neural network, and each layer has its own heads.** A student who gives advice in one class is a head, and the next class is the next layer.
children: Combining the advice gives a better representation of each vector.

sections.title: A dynamical rule across time and depth

teaching.text: **A dynamical system is a rule that is fed back to itself.** Numbers go in, the rule acts on them, and the output is fed back in as the next input, again and again.
children: In the **harmonic oscillator**, x and v **take turns**, the new x computed from the old v and the new v from the new x, and step by step the rule draws a **cosine**.
Fields as far apart as finance use the same idea with different rules.

teaching.text: **Jordan's network was a marriage of neural networks and dynamical systems.** Its **output is copied back into its state units**, and **plan units** and **state units** feed the hidden layer, with the same weights used at every step. After more than **thirty years of tinkering**, this idea became the **LLM**.

**In an LLM, the layer is the rule**, and **depth plays the role of time**. Each layer applies its weights to every vector, and following one number up through the layers traces out a curve, much like the oscillator's curve, though not an exact cosine.
children: The rule in each layer is the weights of its heads, learned through backpropagation by predicting the next word.
The goal is to understand this general structure, not to memorize formulas.

teaching.text: **An LLM is a dynamical system like the oscillator.** In the oscillator, x gives the next v and v gives the next x.
children: An LLM does this with tens of thousands of numbers, many times over.

sections.title: One prediction task for different sequences

teaching.text: An LLM is given **15 vectors** and asked to predict the **16th**, and the vectors can come from anywhere, because the machine only ever sees lists of numbers.
children: They can be **15 words** of a sentence, **15 frames of a spectrogram**, **15 patches of an image** read row by row, or **15 amino acids** in a protein, such as the B chain of insulin.

teaching.text: **The same design and the same prediction game work for language, speech, vision and proteins.**
**The same design was reused by changing what the vectors stand for.** They can be words, pieces of a spectrogram, patches of an image or the amino acids of a protein.
children: One technology solving all of these supports the **horizontal** view, in which every skill uses the same computations.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: Speakers know a small system of **only a few dozen sounds** that decides how vowels and consonants can follow each other, which makes it a good test case for a small LLM. **A simple English syllable is a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**, and only certain **clusters** are allowed, so **sblit**, **lfat** and **desb** are impossible.

**Every language has its own rules for sequences.** Mandarin allows only nasal sounds at the end of a syllable, Cantonese also allows a final p, Russian and Polish allow clusters like zb or dl at the start of a word, and Spanish speakers add an e before a word like stadium.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: Guessing the next letter of an English word reveals this sound knowledge directly. **After a vowel, almost anything can follow**, but **at the start of a word the choices narrow sharply**, so after **sp** only l, r or a vowel can come, and after **skr** only a vowel.

**Guessing the next letter is predicting the 16th vector.** A GPT that only plays this game learns English sounds and spelling, with a **flat** distribution after a vowel and a **sharply peaked** one after skr.

sections.title: Design an agentic system for English syllables

teaching.text: An LLM that learns English syllables can be built by **describing it in English** to an agentic system, specifying **five layers**, **four heads in each layer**, and **input vectors 64 numbers long**, then training it on **1000 English words** to **predict the next letter** and showing ten generated words after each step.
children: The system built a small **character-level transformer** with **attention heads**, where **attention** means a head consults the rest of the sequence to work out which preceding items matter, just as predicting barks requires attending to dog.
After training, the generated words were **still mostly gibberish**, and training on **10,000 words** for many more steps was the suggested next change.

teaching.text: **Software 1.0** is writing programs, **Software 2.0** is letting a network's **weights** become the program, and **Software 3.0** is using an agentic system to build and run a program from plain English, which is called **vibe coding**.

The first attempt at this kind of problem was **Claude Shannon's 1948 paper, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication,"** which generated letter sequences closer and closer to English by hand and founded **information theory**, which remains important for LLMs today.

**An LLM learns by guessing a hidden word and then nudging its weights.** In "The chef cracks the," each word before the gap gives a clue about the hidden word, and these clue relationships are called **interdependencies**.
children: The model does not know the answer, so it spreads its bets. It bets the most on "egg," less on "nut" and the least on "code."
After the true word is revealed, the weights change a little, so the right word gets a bigger bet next time.

teaching.text: **The same idea holds when the signal contains words, sounds and images.** The model still guesses a hidden piece from the other pieces, so only the content of the signal changes.
**Guessing the next word is the GPT task.** The weights are nudged by backpropagation so the guesses improve.
children: Multimodal systems are about two to three years old, and people are multimodal too.

sections.title: Text, speech and images in three different forms

teaching.text: **An LLM can only read a row of vectors, so speech and images have to be converted first.** Text is the easy case because it is already a row of pieces, such as "Now," "crack," "the" and "egg."
children: **Speech is air pressure changing in time**, and there are no words in the sound itself.
**An image is a grid of light**, and it contains no words either.

teaching.text: **The first job is a conversion.** Once speech and images are rows of vectors, one model can read them together with text.
**The words, the speech signal and the image can be three versions of one message.** The speech signal is the pressure variation in front of the mouth.
children: Before multimodal systems, text, speech and vision models were each trained separately.

sections.title: Speech becomes a row of frame vectors

teaching.text: **Speech is turned into a row of vectors by slicing it in time.** Each slice is called a **frame** and is about 20 milliseconds long.
children: The slices go through a **speech encoder**, which is a neural network trained on a large amount of audio. One vector comes out for each slice.

teaching.text: **One second of speech becomes 50 vectors in time order.** Each slice gives one vector, and 50 slices of about 20 milliseconds fill one second.
children: Speech is now a row, just like a sentence, so the LLM can read it one vector after another.

sections.title: Images become a row of patch vectors

teaching.text: **An image is turned into a row of vectors by cutting it into patches.** A **patch** is one small square of the image, and the egg image is cut into 16 of them.
children: The patches are laid out in a row in reading order, so the image becomes a sequence, like a sentence.
A **vision encoder** then gives one vector for each patch.

teaching.text: **Real systems use much smaller patches.** Their patches are 14 to 16 pixels, so one image gives hundreds of vectors.
**Image patches, speech frames and words can all be placed in one row, with the last word hidden.** The words before the gap, "Now," "crack" and "the," still give clues.
children: A patch that contains an egg helps too, and so does the sound of cracking. A link between two different kinds of signal is a **cross-modal dependency**.

teaching.text: **The game is exactly the same as before.** The model guesses the hidden piece from the pieces it can read, and some of the clues now come from other senses.
**The game inside one modality can be played across modalities, because the technology is the same.** The W’s are then about how image patches, speech frames and words relate to one another.
children: After enough training, the W’s are truly multimodal.

sections.title: Three cute puppies as an image, speech and words

teaching.text: **"Three cute puppies" is one event given in three forms.** It is an image cut into 18 patches, the phrase spoken aloud, and the three written words.
children: The spoken phrase is displayed as a **spectrogram**. Time runs from left to right, a higher position means a higher frequency, and a darker area means more energy.
Each thin column of the spectrogram is one frame, and each word sits in its own stretch of time.

teaching.text: **These are three views of one event.** In training, all three go into one row, and the model guesses whichever piece is hidden.
**The example is an ordinary social media post.** It has an image, a caption and a video with the same words spoken.
children: The W’s come from data like this, which is why paying people for their data is being argued.

sections.title: Training example 1 predicts the next word

teaching.text: **In the first training example, the hidden piece is the word after "three cute."** With the words alone, the bets are spread out over "kittens," "puppies" and "babies," because many endings fit.
children: The image contains puppies, and the sound contains the spoken word "puppies." With these clues, the bet piles up on "puppies."

teaching.text: **The model bet 0.85 on the true word, so the nudge to the weights is small.** A large bet on the truth means a small error, and a small error moves the weights only a little.
**The first way gives the system a few words, all the speech and all the patches.** It has to predict the next text word.
children: Its W’s change so that it predicts that word better.

sections.title: Training example 2 predicts a sound frame

teaching.text: **In the second training example, the hidden piece is a frame of sound.** The sound is predicted frame by frame from left to right, which is like teaching the model to speak a sentence it was given.
children: The frames already heard help the most, because the voice and the **formants** (frequency regions with strong energy) change smoothly.
The words say the next sound is the vowel in "pup," and the image backs up the words.

teaching.text: **A frame is a column of numbers for the energy in each frequency band.** The guess is close but not exact, and the error between the guess and the truth nudges the weights.
**The second way gives the system the patches, the words and half of the speech.** It has to predict the next bit of speech.
children: It uses the speech frames, the words and the patches together.

sections.title: Training example 3 predicts an image patch

teaching.text: **In the third training example, the hidden piece is a patch of the image.** The patches are predicted in reading order, which is like teaching the model to draw what it was told.
children: The patches already drawn give background above and two puppies to the left. "Three" says a third puppy must appear, and "puppies" says to expect dog ears.
The sound carries the same words, so it backs up the text.

teaching.text: **The biggest error is the colour.** The model guesses an ear in the average colour of the first two puppies, but the third puppy is dark, and no clue said so.
children: Only systems that also produce images are trained this way.

teaching.text: **The third way asks for the next patch, which is the third dog.** Two dogs alone could be followed by a kennel or a person.
children: The words and the speech both say “three puppies,” so a third puppy has the highest probability.

sections.title: Every piece can be the hidden one

teaching.text: **Any piece of the row can be the hidden one, and each sense gives a clue for it.** For a hidden word, "three cute" calls for a plural noun, the word was just spoken, and the image contains puppies.
children: For a hidden frame, the words say which sound comes next, the voice and formants carry on, and the image backs up the word.
For a hidden patch, "three" says one more puppy is coming, the sound gives the same words, and the fur and background carry on.

teaching.text: **A clue from the same sense says how the signal continues, and clues from the other senses say what the thing is.** So each sense fills gaps that the others leave, which is why training on all three together helps.
**One post trains the system in every direction.** It goes from speech and vision to text, from text and vision to speech, and so on.
children: **W’s are knowledge**, and here the knowledge is about the bond between speaking, hearing and seeing.

sections.title: Talking back, and what is new

teaching.text: **For the model to speak, sound is compressed into discrete codes that work like new words in the vocabulary.** The model predicts the next code exactly as it predicts the next word.
children: A **decoder** then turns the codes back into a sound wave.

teaching.text: **Three things are new, and the learning rule stays the same.** The new things are a shared currency of vectors in one row, data where the senses appear together, and a schedule that protects what was already learned.
children: What stays the same is finding the dependencies in the signal. The signal has only become wider.

teaching.text: **A modality is like a sense, and language counts as one.** Separate LLMs for language, speech, vision and biology have been combined over the last three or four years.
children: Biomedical multimodal LLMs combine scans, notes, lab results and sequences. An ordinary chat system already knows about a hundred languages.
